titulo: Estaba buenísimo — and the cook comes out
subtitulo: The four words that get you the recommendation the house really makes, a thank you that gets heard, one word for a raised glass, and the quiet sentence that sorts a cold plate out in ten seconds
cena: Half eleven at night, the plates went ten minutes ago, the card machine is on its way to your table, and the woman who cooked what you have just eaten is four steps away behind a bead curtain.
decisao: whether the four words get said before you pay — the table that names the dish gets the recommendation the house really makes, the welcome back on Thursday and, in a small place, sometimes the round nobody charged for; and the plate that arrived cold either gets sorted in ten seconds or gets paid for in silence

clique.desconto: Nobody gave you those sentences. You made them on the spot, out of two openers, and the shortest of them is two words long.
clique.piso: You will tell a Spanish kitchen that what it made was good, and be understood. Most visitors spend a fortnight eating well and never say so to anybody.

frasePiso: You will tell a Spanish kitchen that what it made was good, and be understood. Most visitors spend a fortnight eating well and never say so to anybody.
permissao: You are allowed to say two words and stop — no speech, no list, and no sorry in front of it. You are allowed to praise the food with your mouth full, which is when it is usually said. And you are allowed to send a cold plate back without apologising for it: saying so is information, not a scene, and it is over in ten seconds.
espelho: Thanking at every single turn is the bit that reads as odd there. Spent that often it stops being warmth and starts being distance — one, at the end, meant, is worth all six of them.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You say the food was good, the waiter says almost nothing, turns round and disappears through a curtain at the back.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: I have said it wrong, or he is not interested, and now I have made the whole thing awkward.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: In a house where one person is cooking, that sentence is information the kitchen wants, so somebody carries it through. Coming out to hear it again is the ordinary end of it, not a ceremony.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Stay where you are for half a minute and say it again to the person who made it, with the name of the dish at the front.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get the recommendation the house actually makes instead of the safe one, and the table is remembered when you walk back in on Thursday.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not where forty tables are served off one pass and the plates leave through a hatch — there it stops at the waiter, nobody comes out, and nothing has gone wrong.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You put a please and a thank you on every single turn, and the person serving you answers the first one and lets the rest go past.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: They are being short with me, or I have done something to annoy them.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Thanks lands at the end of an exchange rather than inside every beat of it. Spent at every turn it reads as ceremony, and ceremony puts distance exactly where you were trying to close it.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Spend one, at the end, looking at them, and put 'de verdad' on it when you mean it.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: The one you do spend is heard, and you stop sounding like somebody being handled at a counter.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not when somebody has gone out of their way — walked you round the corner, rung a taxi, held a shop open past closing. There you thank properly, twice, and it is not too much.

fichasCulturais.sinal: A plate lands cold, and at the next table the same thing is sorted in ten seconds with nobody's voice going up.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: Saying anything is going to turn into a scene, so I will eat it and say nothing.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: A flat statement of fact — this is cold, this is not what I asked for — is heard as information, and putting it right is routine work. What is read badly is the performance around it, not the request.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Say the fact in the voice you order in, sitting down, and then ask for the thing that fixes it. No apology in front.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You eat what you actually ordered, and the temperature of the room does not change at all.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not an allergy. That one is not a preference to be sorted with a smile — it is the flat, serious sentence from part thirteen, and it never gets this easy voice.

steps.pt: Part twenty-five. Warm-up: the punch. One syllable takes it, and only one. Bue-NÍ-si-mo. Ri-QUÍ-si-mo.
Four beats, the second one hit hard, the last two small and still there. Hand on your leg, twice more.

steps.promptPt: Twenty-five minutes since the last plate went, everybody is chatting, and nobody is coming near you — because here nobody ever will. Speak now.
steps.pt: it is never coming otherwise
Half eleven at night. The plates went ten minutes ago and the card machine is on its way over.
Four steps behind you, through a bead curtain, is the woman who cooked what you have just eaten.
You are going to pay and walk out, and the whole evening will have happened without her hearing a word.
👂 'How is it all?' — asked halfway through, and it is not small talk.
That is a door being held open, and almost every visitor answers it with a nod. Two words fit through it.
It was delicious. — about a plate you have finished.
That is the frame. Estaba, and then what you thought of it. The front of it never moves.
The other word for it. Both are ordinary, and both land.
The list is the list: six of them, learnt whole, so there is nothing to work out at a table.

steps.promptPt: The plates are gone from the restaurant table, the owner is stood there with the card machine, and that fish was the best thing you have eaten all week. Tell him, before you pay. Speak now.
steps.pt: what you thought of it
Watch what he does with that. He does not say much. He turns round and goes to the back.
👂 'Did you like the rice?' — the kitchen has been told, and now it has come out to hear it.
The same two words with the name of the thing in front of them — four words in all.

steps.promptPt: She has come out of the kitchen wiping her hands, and she is waiting to hear you name the thing she made. Put its name at the front. Speak now.
steps.pt: with its name at the front
Four words now, not two. Naming it is the whole difference: the one who names it gets talked to.

steps.pinyin: meh PWEH-dheh deh-THEER KOH-moh seh YAH-mah
steps.pt: Could you tell me what it is called? — the opener from part three, with a new ending on it.
You already own the front of that one, from part three. Only what hangs off the end is new tonight.

steps.promptPt: Something arrived with the second round that you never ordered and cannot name, and you want it again tomorrow in another town. He is clearing the next table. Speak now.
steps.pinyin: meh PWEH-dheh deh-THEER KOH-moh seh YAH-mah
steps.pt: so you can ask for it again
There is a shorter one for when your mouth is full, and that is exactly when it gets said.
'How good is that!' — two words, and you can say it chewing.
The same one with the other word in it. Either does the job.
Qué, and then what you think of it. Two words, and it fits between two bites.

steps.promptPt: Standing at the counter, a plate of small things between you, and you have just bitten into the one with egg in it. Mouth full, two words. Speak now.
steps.pt: two words, mouth full
'That looks good!' — said to a plate as it lands, and to the person carrying it.

steps.promptPt: A tray goes past your table on its way to somebody else, and the smell of it arrives first. Say it to the man carrying it, before he is gone. Speak now.
steps.pt: to the plate, and to the man carrying it
The same opener takes what is around you, not just what is in front of you. One word rides in the middle.
'What a lovely spot!' — the patio, the bar, the room they have just walked you into.

steps.promptPt: They have walked you through the bar and out into a courtyard with a lemon tree in it, and the owner is watching your face. Speak now.
steps.pt: about the room you are standing in
And the end of the word moves with the thing in front of it. You take that by ear, never by rule.
The same one about all of it. Bonita here, bonito there — nobody minds either way.

steps.promptPt: Twenty minutes in a taxi in from the station, the river on your left, and the driver has asked what you make of it so far. Speak now.
steps.pt: about all of it, not just the street
One more, and it has nothing to do with food. It is for the person who has gone out of their way.
'How kind!' — for the man who walked you round the corner, or the girl who rang the taxi.

steps.promptPt: The girl at the hotel desk has just spent four minutes on the phone getting you a table for tonight, and she is holding the door open for you. Speak now.
steps.pt: about her, not the food
The version you say on your way out. Warmer than gracias on its own, and just as short.
At home you thank at every turn. Here that many of them reads as ceremony, and ceremony is distance.
So spend one. At the end, looking at them, with two words on it that hardly any visitor says.
'Thank you, really.' — the last two words are what make it land.

steps.promptPt: You are at the door on the way out, and the evening was far better than it had any business being. Say it once, and mean the end of it. Speak now.
steps.pt: the one that gets heard
GUIRI ALERT. George here. The British compliment, in full: 'Sorry — that was actually really lovely, thanks so much.'
Four hedges and an apology, delivered to a man's back while he carries the plates away. He heard none of it.
Two words, to a face, out loud. Qué rico. That one gets carried into the kitchen. Mine died at the table.
Glasses go up before the first sip. One word does it, and it is the shortest thing you learn today.
'Cheers!' — up, out, and then you drink.

steps.promptPt: Four of you round a small table, the first round has landed, and everybody has a hand on a glass waiting for somebody to start it off. Speak now.
steps.pt: up, and then you drink
'Enjoy your meal' — to anybody eating, including strangers you walk past.

steps.promptPt: You are squeezing past a table on your way out and the couple sat there have just been served. Two words as you pass. Speak now.
steps.pt: two words, in passing
Now the other half of the same skill, in the same voice. Something has landed at your table cold.
There will be no scene. A scene here buys you a shrug. The table sorts this in about ten seconds.
'Sorry — this is cold.' A fact. Nobody has been accused of anything yet.

steps.promptPt: The soup has been in front of you for a minute and it is barely warm, and he is still stood there with the tray. Say what it is, and nothing else. Speak now.
steps.pt: the fact, and nothing else

steps.es: Uy, perdona. ¿Te lo cambio o te lo caliento?
steps.pinyin: OO-ee, pehr-DOH-nah. teh loh KAM-byoh oh teh loh kah-LYEN-toh
steps.pt: 👂 'Sorry! Shall I change it or heat it up?' — pick one. Nobody is upset with you.
steps.tts: Uy, perdona. ¿Te lo cambio o te lo caliento?

steps.pt: Then the ask, and it is the opener from part three again, with something new hanging off the end.

steps.pinyin: meh loh PWEH-dheh kam-BYAR, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: 'Could you change it for me, please?' — the 'me lo' rides on the front as one word.

steps.promptPt: He has had a look at the plate and he agrees with you. Ask him for the thing that fixes it, in the same voice you have ordered in all evening. Speak now.
steps.pinyin: meh loh PWEH-dheh kam-BYAR, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: the ask that fixes it
No apology in front, no speech behind. He takes it away, and the evening carries on as it was.
The same flat voice works on paper, when there is a line at the bottom that nobody mentioned.

steps.es: Aquí hay un cargo que no estaba en la carta. ¿Qué es?
steps.pinyin: ah-KEE ai oon KAR-goh keh noh ehs-TAH-bah en lah KAR-tah. keh ehs
steps.pt: 'There is a charge here that was not on the menu. What is it?' — from part fourteen, said sitting down.
steps.tts: Aquí hay un cargo que no estaba en la carta. ¿Qué es?

steps.promptPt: The total at the bottom has something in it you never ordered, and you are still sat down and still calm. Name it, ask for nothing yet, and wait. Speak now.
steps.es: Aquí hay un cargo que no estaba en la carta. ¿Qué es?
steps.pinyin: ah-KEE ai oon KAR-goh keh noh ehs-TAH-bah en lah KAR-tah. keh ehs
steps.pt: name it and wait
That is as far as it goes tonight. The rest of that ladder you already own, from part fourteen.
Back to the man who walked off. He was not being short with you and he was not ignoring you.
Where one person is cooking, that sentence is worth carrying, so somebody carries it through the curtain.
Not where forty tables are served through a hatch. There it stops at the waiter, and nothing has gone wrong.
You can say two words and stop. No speech, no list, no sorry in front of it, and you can say it chewing.
And thanking at every single turn is the bit that reads as odd there. One, at the end, meant, beats six.
Count the places. The restaurant table. The counter. The courtyard. The taxi. The hotel desk.
Nobody gave you those sentences. You made them on the spot, out of two openers, and the shortest is two words.
You will tell a Spanish kitchen that what it made was good, and be understood. Most visitors never say it at all.
Shadowing. Out loud, underneath them, flat vowels and one punch a word. The two you will use daily:
It was delicious.
How good is that!
One more out loud, somewhere we have not stood yet, and this time nobody has asked you anything.

steps.promptPt: A market stall, and the woman has cut a sliver off the wheel and put it in your hand without being asked. It is still in your mouth. Speak now.
steps.pt: with your mouth full
That is it. You said it, they heard it, and the cold plate went back with nobody's voice going up. Hasta luego.

aprofundar.titulo: Saying it, meaning it, and sending it back (optional reading)

secoes.titulo: Estaba, not está — and why the -ísimo does the work
secoes.corpo: About a plate you have finished, the natural thing to say is 'estaba buenísimo': the food was good while it lasted, and it has now stopped existing. 'Está buenísimo' is what you say with a fork still in it. Both are correct and nobody will blink at either, so this is not a rule to hold in your head at the table — it is simply why the recorded version says estaba. The ending -ísimo is a whole extra layer of enthusiasm bolted onto the adjective: bueno becomes buenísimo, rico becomes riquísimo (the c hardens to a qu so the sound stays the same). It is very common, it is not childish or over the top, and it is the single cheapest way to sound like you meant it rather than like you are being polite. One warning worth having: 'soy bueno' about yourself does not mean you are a good person, and 'estoy buena' about yourself is a comment on your looks. The food gets buenísimo; leave your own adjectives alone.

exemplos.pt: ehs-TAH-bah TOH-dhoh bweh-NEE-see-moh — everything was delicious (the whole-table version, at the end of a meal)
ehs-TAH rree-KEE-see-moh — this is delicious (with the fork still in your hand)

secoes.titulo: ¡Qué + the thing + más + the word! — one shape, four uses
secoes.corpo: The second half of the frame is even shorter: ¡Qué rico! ¡Qué bueno! ¡Qué amable! Two words and three beats, which is why it survives a mouthful of tortilla. When you want to say it about a thing rather than about the taste, the thing goes in the middle and 'más' props it up: ¡Qué sitio más bonito! ¡Qué ciudad más bonita! ¡Qué plaza más bonita! The ending of the last word follows the thing in the middle — bonito for sitio, bonita for ciudad — and this is the one place where you take it by ear and refuse to think about it. Getting it the wrong way round costs you precisely nothing: it is heard as an accent, not as an error, and the compliment arrives intact. You can also drop 'más' entirely (¡Qué sitio bonito!) and it still works. Two more that come free: '¡Qué buena pinta!' is said to a plate as it lands — la pinta is the look of a thing — and '¡Qué rico está esto!' is the long version of the short one, for when you have time.

exemplos.pt: keh PLAH-thah mahs boh-NEE-tah — what a lovely square
keh ah-MAH-bleh — how kind, thank you very much (for a person, never for food)

secoes.titulo: The thank you that gets heard
secoes.corpo: British courtesy spends a please and a thank you on every turn of an exchange, and in Spain that count reads as ceremony — not rude, but formal, and formality at a counter is distance. The local shape is one, at the end, meant: 'muchas gracias' with your eyes up, and 'de verdad' on the end when the person actually did something for you. 'Muy amable' — you're very kind — is the other one, and it is the natural reply when somebody has gone out of their way. The exception runs the other way and it matters: when somebody has genuinely put themselves out, walked you three streets, rung a taxi, opened up after closing, then thank them properly and twice, and nothing about that is too much. What you are trading is quantity for weight. Bank one more, for the room rather than the person: 'que aproveche' is what you say to people who are eating as you pass them, and it is said between strangers all day long. Waiters say it when the food lands; you say it on your way out.

exemplos.pt: deh behr-DAHDH — thank you, really. The two words on the end are the whole point
keh ah-proh-BEH-cheh — enjoy your meal, said in passing to anybody eating

secoes.titulo: The glass, and what not to make of it
secoes.corpo: '¡Salud!' is the toast, it is one word, and it covers every table you will sit at. Glasses go up, you say it, you drink. There is no speech, no clinking ritual you have to get right, and no round-the-table order to learn. If somebody says something longer and you did not catch it, '¡Salud!' back is a complete and correct answer. Two neighbours of it that you will hear and never need to produce: 'que vaya bien' is said to somebody leaving, and 'que aproveche' is the one for eating. What we are deliberately not doing here is turning a toast into a performance: the whole social weight of it is in raising the glass and looking up, and the word is just the noise that goes with it. The evening at somebody's home — what to take, where to sit, when to leave, and how to accept the invitation in the first place — is a part of its own further on.

exemplos.pt: sah-LOODH — cheers. One word, every table, every time
keh BAH-yah byen — 👂 all the best, said to somebody heading off

secoes.titulo: Sending something back without it becoming an event
secoes.corpo: The sentence that works is a flat statement of fact with nobody in it: 'Perdone, esto está frío.' There is no accusation, no story about how long you waited and no apology in front of it, which is exactly why it gets a quick fix rather than a defensive one. Other endings for the same shape: 'esto no es lo que he pedido' (this is not what I ordered), 'esto está crudo' (this is underdone), 'esta copa está sucia' (this glass is dirty). Then the ask, which is an opener you already own: '¿Me lo puede cambiar?' — the me lo travels on the front of it as if it were part of the word, and you never take it apart. Volume and posture do more than vocabulary here: stay sitting, keep the voice you order in, and let the fact stand on its own. A tourist performing outrage is theatre and is treated as theatre; a customer stating a fact is work, and work gets done. If it is a line on the bill rather than a plate, the ladder from part fourteen takes over — the itemised bill first, then naming the charge, then the complaint form — and it is the same voice all the way up. And the one thing that never gets this easy register is an allergy: that is the flat, serious sentence from part thirteen, said looking at them, with the card in your hand.

exemplos.es: Perdone, esto no es lo que he pedido.
exemplos.pt: noh es loh keh eh peh-DEE-dhoh — sorry, this is not what I ordered
meh loh PWEH-dheh kam-BYAR — could you change it for me, please?

secoes.titulo: Tú, usted, and who you are talking to when you say it
secoes.corpo: The compliments in this part are the same words whoever you are talking to, which is half the reason they are the ones we chose: 'estaba buenísimo' and '¡qué rico!' carry no decision about the person opposite. Only two sentences here lean either way. '¿Le ha gustado el arroz?' is what you will hear from an older waiter or in a more formal dining room — le is the usted version — and you do not have to answer in kind; naming the dish is the answer. And '¿Me lo puede cambiar?' is the same shape you learned in part three for '¿me lo puede escribir?' — we recorded it that way so the opener you already know does not change on you halfway through the course, not because a restaurant demands it. In a young bar the tú version, '¿me lo puedes cambiar?', is flying about all evening, and if somebody uses tú with you, use it back. Nothing in this part breaks if you get it the other way round.

exemplos.pt: teh ah goos-TAH-dhoh — 👂 the tú version of the same question, in a younger place
meh loh PWEH-dhehs kam-BYAR — the tú version of the ask, for a bar where you are already on tú
